storySeeds.title: Stars that change: a Cepheus–Cassiopeia–Perseus circuit
storySeeds.region: Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Perseus (about 25° radius around Cassiopeia)
storySeeds.description: Start with δ Cephei and the observing task EarthSky suggests: judge it against ζ and ε Cephei. Move to the Garnet Star (slow, irregular), ρ Cas (outbursts), γ Cas (a disk that comes and goes), and finish on Algol, with Almach and ε Persei as the brightness yardsticks from EarthSky’s Algol guide. Comparison method from the BAA Variable Star Section beginners’ page. Payoff: one region, four different reasons a star changes.

storySeeds.title: How big can a star be? Giants of Cepheus
storySeeds.description: A hot, heavy young star (10 Lac) and a nursery (IC 1396) set up the question; the Garnet Star, VV Cephei and RW Cephei answer it with three of the largest stars in binocular reach, each measured a different way (spectra, eclipses, interferometer images). Coda: Alderamin, a small star squashed by its spin. Ground: APOD on μ Cep, Baines et al. 2021, Anugu et al. 2023.

storySeeds.title: Worlds around other suns
storySeeds.description: 51 Pegasi (the first planet found around a Sun-like star) → HD 209458 (the first transit) → υ Andromedae (the first multi-planet system) → the Andromeda Galaxy as the scale payoff. A variant opens on Errai, the 1988 hint that came too early. NASA’s exoplanet page for 51 Peg b and the discovery papers supply the facts.

storySeeds.title: Rings at both ends of life: Fomalhaut, the Helix and the dim neighbors
storySeeds.region: Piscis Austrinus and Aquarius (about 20° radius; best below 40° N)
storySeeds.description: Fomalhaut’s debris rings (Webb) against the Helix, a dying star’s shell, with two of the nearest red dwarfs as the twist: closer than Fomalhaut but invisible to the eye. EarthSky’s Fomalhaut guide supplies the find-it route from the Great Square; NASA’s Webb release the disk story.

card.question: Why does Algol, the Demon Star, lose two-thirds of its light every few days?
card.glance: A white star in Perseus that looks perfectly ordinary until, every few days, it slips to a third of its usual brightness for a few hours.
card.whyHere: Algol is the easiest star in the sky to catch in the act of changing, and the cause has nothing to do with the star itself.
card.see: Algol sits in Perseus, about halfway between Cassiopeia’s W and the Pleiades, and your eyes alone can follow it. At full light it matches Almach, the golden star at the end of Andromeda; deep in eclipse it sinks to the level of ε Persei.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars, with a third circling farther out, and we see the pair’s orbit almost edge-on: an eclipsing binary. Every 2.87 days the dim orange companion slides across the hot blue-white star. The shape of the change gives it away: a pulsing star brightens and fades all the time, while Algol holds steady for most of its cycle and then drops sharply for a few hours, just as a passing body would make it.
card.wonder: Algol's dimmer partner is the lighter star yet the more aged one, because it swelled first and poured much of its gas onto its partner, turning the former heavyweight into the lightweight.
card.connect: Mira and δ Cephei change for the opposite reason: the star itself swells and shrinks.
card.answer: Neither star changes; the fainter one simply passes in front of the brighter and blocks most of its light until it moves on. The Demon’s wink is a shadow play, staged nearly 90 light-years away.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo freezes Algol at one moment, so it cannot show the eclipse. Interferometers have imaged the pair, but only as a few pixels.
card.deeper: Kolbas et al. (2015) separated the three spectra: Algol A is a B8 dwarf of 3.39 solar masses at about 12,550 K; Algol B is a cool subgiant of 0.77 solar masses; Algol C (1.58 solar masses) orbits the pair every 680 days. The “Algol paradox” — the less massive star is the more evolved — is explained by mass transfer: B was once the heavier star, aged first and handed much of its gas to A. CHARA interferometry resolved the inner pair (Baron et al. 2012). Hipparcos parallax: 36.3 ± 1.4 mas.

card.question: How can one star be easy to see one season and invisible months later?
card.glance: A red star in the neck of Cetus, the Whale, which is either an obvious naked-eye star or lost even to binoculars, depending on the month.
card.whyHere: Mira is an old red giant caught in the act of pulsing, the clearest preview in the sky of the Sun’s own old age.
card.see: Check a current brightness estimate first, because Mira may be out of reach tonight. Near its peak it is an obvious orange-red point in the Whale’s neck, well south of Aries; judge it quickly, since red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
card.understand: Mira is a red giant, a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to hundreds of times the Sun’s width, and every 332 days it swells and shrinks. That alone would change its light only modestly. The trick is its cool surface, around 3,000 K, where molecules form and break apart with each pulse, and when they form they soak up visible light like a curtain drawn across a window.
card.wonder: Mira races through space trailing a wake of shed gas about 13 light-years long, recorded in ultraviolet by NASA’s GALEX satellite: some 30,000 years of its history written across the sky.
card.connect: The gas it sheds will drift off to seed new stars, and once a star like Mira has lost everything, it ends as a glowing shell like the Helix Nebula.
card.answer: The pulse draws that curtain open and shut, so at its best Mira sends us more than a thousand times the light of its faintest. David Fabricius watched it vanish in 1596, yet it has kept coming back ever since.
card.photoCaption: Hubble’s ultraviolet image shows Mira and its hot companion as two smudges; to the eye it is one red point whose brightness depends on the date.
card.deeper: Near-infrared interferometry (Woodruff et al. 2004) gives a diameter of about 330–400 solar radii and 2,900–3,200 K, both varying with phase; the size also depends on wavelength because of molecular layers. The companion, Mira B, about half an arcsecond away, is a white dwarf feeding on Mira’s wind (Sokoloski & Bildsten 2010). The GALEX tail was reported by Martin et al. (2007). Hipparcos parallax 10.9 ± 1.2 mas (about 270–340 light-years). Period 332 days (GCVS).

eventDependent.note: Mira changes by a factor of hundreds over its cycle and is often below binocular reach. Check a current estimate before you go.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.whyHere: William Herschel likened its color to a garnet, and it is the clearest proof in the sky that color is a star’s thermometer.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows a saturated point in a rich Milky Way field beside the faint glow of IC 1396; its disk is far too small to see in any ordinary image.
card.deeper: The distance is the weak link: published values span roughly 390–870 pc, and Wiesemeyer et al. (2026) adopt 421 (+57/−42) pc. The radius scales with distance. Perrin et al. (2005) measured a photospheric diameter of 14.1 mas inside a larger molecular shell, which gives about 600–1,300 solar radii across that range; Levesque et al. (2005) found about 3,700 K and 1,420 solar radii for their adopted distance. B−V of 2.35 (SIMBAD) makes it one of the reddest naked-eye stars.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness drifts over months; compare it with neighboring stars instead of trusting a printed magnitude.

card.question: How did a star that pulses every five days become a ruler for the universe?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a blue-white companion beside it, brightening and fading on a strict five-day rhythm.
card.whyHere: δ Cephei gave its name to the Cepheids, the pulsing stars whose beat became the first yardstick for distances beyond our galaxy.
card.see: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Over several nights compare it with ζ Cephei, its match at peak, and ε Cephei, its match at the bottom, and you will see it brighten quickly and fade slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life, and its outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied many such stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, all at nearly the same distance, so any difference in how bright they looked had to be real. The slower a star beat, she found, the brighter it truly was: time the pulse and you know its real power.
card.wonder: Its cousins in distant galaxies still anchor the measurement of how fast the universe is expanding.
card.connect: β Cephei, elsewhere in the same constellation, pulses too, but every few hours and so gently that only instruments can tell.
card.answer: Know a lamp’s true wattage, and how faint it looks tells you how far away it is. When Edwin Hubble caught the same beat in a star inside the Andromeda “nebula”, the universe grew enormously overnight.
card.photoCaption: The survey image shows δ Cephei and its companion as two points. Seeing the pulse needs your own eyes over several nights, not a photograph.
card.deeper: HST astrometry gave a parallax of 3.66 ± 0.15 mas, about 273 pc (Benedict et al. 2002); a Hipparcos reanalysis gives 244 ± 10 pc and revealed a close spectroscopic companion (Anderson et al. 2015). Nardetto et al. (2024) used that orbit to weigh the Cepheid at about 5.3 solar masses. Gallenne et al. (2021) find about 1,950 solar luminosities. The period is 5.366 days and the visual range 3.48–4.37 (GCVS). Goodricke published the discovery in 1786.

card.question: How can an eclipse measure a star too distant to see as a disk?
card.glance: A modest orange star in Cepheus that shows no sign of being two stars, one of them enormous.
card.whyHere: VV Cephei is a red supergiant with a hot blue partner, and the pair’s rare eclipses let astronomers size up a giant star by timing alone.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees north of the Garnet Star, so sweep between the two and compare them. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery, and its slow changes are too small to judge by eye.
card.understand: The star you see is a red supergiant, a heavyweight in the bloated last stage of its life, and a hot blue star circles it on an orbit we see nearly edge-on. Once every 20.3 years the giant swings in front of its partner and hides it for a long stretch. Knowing the blue star’s speed from its light, astronomers can treat the eclipse like a car passing behind a long wall: speed multiplied by time gives the length of the wall.
card.wonder: Its eclipses are among the longest known, the blue star staying hidden behind the giant for well over a year.
card.connect: Algol’s wink every few days and VV Cephei’s twenty-year eclipse are the same geometry, with only the size of the stars and their orbit changed.
card.answer: The hidden star acts as a probe, and pacing out its passage behind the giant gives the giant’s width almost directly. Interferometers, which read its tiny disk, put it at hundreds of times the Sun’s width.
card.photoCaption: No ordinary photo separates the two stars; they are far too close. The app’s size diagram shows the giant against the planets’ orbits instead.
card.deeper: Baines et al. (2021) measured the giant’s angular diameter with the Navy Precision Optical Interferometer: about 779 solar radii and 73,000 solar luminosities at the Gaia DR3 distance. Gaia-based distances (Bailer-Jones et al. 2021) give about 1,020 (+140/−100) pc; older radius estimates reach 1,050 solar radii or more, so treat the size as uncertain by tens of percent. The orbit (Wright 1977) has a period of 7,430 days and an eccentricity of 0.35.

eventDependent.note: Its long eclipses come once every 20.3 years and it also varies slightly between them; check AAVSO for its current state.

radiusRsun.note: interferometric diameter at the adopted distance

superlatives.claim: one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye

historyHook.text: In 2000 it suddenly dimmed and cooled while throwing off a shell of gas about 10,000 times Earth’s mass.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae is a yellow hypergiant, a star at the very top of the power scale, and a lesson in how badly faintness can mislead.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of Caroline’s Rose between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only a point of light. The 2000 outburst was found in its spectrum, not in pictures.
card.deeper: Kasikov et al. (2026) adopt 2.81 ± 0.10 kpc from its stellar group and log L/L☉ = 5.83 (+0.12/−0.16), with an interferometric radius of about 630 solar radii. Lobel et al. (2003) followed the 2000–2001 outburst spectroscopically: the atmosphere cooled sharply and briefly lost mass at around 5 × 10⁻² solar masses per year, about 3% of a solar mass in all. Gorlova et al. (2006) estimate about 40 solar masses. Many astronomers think it has already been a red supergiant and is now heating up again.

eventDependent.note: It brightens and fades irregularly and has had sudden outbursts; check AAVSO rather than relying on a printed magnitude.

superlatives.claim: the first star found to show bright emission lines in its spectrum (1866)

historyHook.text: In 1866 Angelo Secchi saw bright lines in its spectrum — the first time anyone had seen them in a star.

card.question: Why has the middle star of Cassiopeia’s W brightened and faded over the decades?
card.glance: The blue-white center star of Cassiopeia’s W, plain to look at but wrapped in a disk of glowing gas.
card.whyHere: γ Cassiopeiae is the original Be star, a hot young star spinning so fast that it sheds gas from its waist.
card.see: γ Cas is the middle star of the W, a clean blue-white point in binoculars. Swing to orange Schedar, the next bright star west, and back: over the decades γ has sometimes outshone Schedar and sometimes fallen below it, so your comparison tonight joins a long record.
card.understand: γ Cas is about 8 million years old, many times heavier than the Sun, and spinning so fast that its equator barely holds on. Gas leaks off that bulging equator into a flattened disk, like mud flung from a spinning wheel. In 1866 Angelo Secchi spread its light into a spectrum and saw bright lines where dark ones belong, a first for any star, and those lines come from the glowing disk.
card.wonder: Its light set out in the late Middle Ages, so tonight you see the disk it wore more than five centuries ago.
card.connect: Spin shapes stars: Alderamin in Cepheus is flattened by its spin, and γ Cas spins hard enough to shed a disk.
card.answer: The star stays much the same while its disk comes and goes, adding its glow as it builds and taking it away as it thins. That is why the W’s middle star has wandered between about magnitudes 1.6 and 3.0.
card.photoCaption: No photograph is shown: the gas disk is far too small for any ordinary image. Its story is written in its spectrum.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 5.94 ± 0.12 mas (about 550 light-years). Classified B0.5 IVpe. GCVS lists a visual range of 1.6–3.0 as the disk built up and dissipated over the 20th century. Isochrone fitting gives an age of about 8 million years (Tetzlaff et al. 2011). Secchi’s report of bright Hβ in 1866 (published 1867) made it the first emission-line star.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness has wandered between about 1.6 and 3.0 over the decades as its disk grows and fades; compare it with Schedar tonight.

superlatives.claim: the brightest star of the Alpha Persei Cluster

card.question: Why is Mirfak yellower than the blue-white stars that surround it?
card.glance: The brightest star of Perseus, yellow-white and ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.whyHere: Mirfak is the brightest member of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a young star family that fits in one binocular view and shows two stages of life at once.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia’s W, and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains, with Mirfak a shade yellower than the rest. Wide, low-power binoculars frame this cluster better than any telescope.
card.understand: An open cluster is a family of stars born together from one gas cloud, so its members share a birthday and a distance. That makes it a natural experiment in which the one big difference is how much mass each star started with. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so the heaviest runs out of core hydrogen first and swells while its lighter siblings carry on.
card.wonder: Mirfak and its siblings still travel through space together, a family that has stayed close for tens of millions of years.
card.connect: In the older Pleiades, stars as heavy as Mirfak have already burned out.
card.answer: Mirfak started out the heaviest of the family, about seven times the Sun’s mass, so it has already swollen into a yellow supergiant while its siblings still shine blue-white, all within some tens of millions of years.
card.photoCaption: Photos of the cluster record many faint members; in binoculars the brightest blue-white ones stand out around yellow Mirfak.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 6.44 ± 0.17 mas (about 510 light-years). Lyubimkov et al. (2010) derived about 6,350 K, 7.3 solar masses and a single-star model age of about 41 million years from spectroscopy and evolutionary tracks, younger than the 50–90 million years other methods give the cluster, a known tension between star models and cluster clocks. Spectral type F5 Ib. Cluster ages from other methods are discussed on the Alpha Persei Cluster stop.

distanceLy.note: 3.4 kpc if a Cepheus OB1 member; Gaia allows 3.4–6.7 kpc

radiusRsun.note: from the CHARA angular diameter over the distance range

superlatives.claim: one of the largest known stars in the Milky Way

card.question: Why did one of the largest stars in the galaxy suddenly fade?
card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.whyHere: RW Cephei is one of the largest stars known in our galaxy, and it recently went through its own great dimming, much as Betelgeuse did.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-south-west of δ Cephei, and binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so note it against the stars around it.
card.understand: RW Cep is a hypergiant, an exceptionally heavy and luminous star swollen in a late, unstable stage. The CHARA array combines several telescopes into what acts like one giant instrument, and it shows a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During the recent fade one side looked darker than the other, which is not how a star that dims evenly would look.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left it about 11,000 years ago, around when people first began to farm.
card.connect: The Garnet Star, a few degrees away, is a red supergiant of the same size class, still shining unveiled.
card.answer: RW Cephei threw off gas that cooled into dust on one side, and the cloud blocked part of its light, much as a dusty veil dimmed Betelgeuse in 2019 and 2020. The star kept shining; a curtain had been drawn across our view.
card.photoCaption: Ordinary photos show a point. Infrared images from the CHARA Array, only a few pixels across, revealed the darkened half.
card.deeper: Anugu et al. (2023) reconstructed CHARA images during the dimming. Their angular diameter implies 900–1,760 solar radii, depending on distance: about 3.4 kpc if it belongs to Cepheus OB1, with Gaia allowing 3.4–6.7 kpc. They attribute the fading to a recent surface mass ejection that formed dust in front of the star, similar to Betelgeuse in 2019–2020. GCVS lists it as an irregular supergiant variable (6.2–8.0).

eventDependent.note: It fades and recovers irregularly; check AAVSO before comparing it with neighboring stars.

superlatives.claim: one of the reddest stars visible to the naked eye

card.question: What makes a carbon star so much redder than other red giants?
card.glance: A strongly orange-red star just east of the Circlet of Pisces, one of the reddest stars visible to the naked eye.
card.whyHere: TX Piscium is a carbon star, an old giant whose atmosphere is laced with carbon made deep inside it, and it wears one of the richest colors in the sky.
card.see: Find the Circlet, a faint ring of stars south of the Great Square of Pegasus; TX Piscium is the ruddy star just east of it, standing out at once beside the white field stars. Look away and back again, because red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
card.understand: TX Psc is a giant near the end of its life, about 295 times wider than the Sun, with a surface of only about 3,100 K. Deep inside, helium fuses into carbon in bursts, and churning currents dredge the new carbon up to the surface. In most stars oxygen outnumbers carbon and locks it away in carbon monoxide, but once carbon wins that count, the leftover carbon is free to build other molecules and soot.
card.wonder: Much of the carbon in your body was made in stars like this one and blown into space by their winds.
card.connect: Its soot will drift off to seed future stars and planets, and the Helix Nebula shows the shell such a star finally leaves.
card.answer: That spare carbon forms molecules and soot that soak up blue and violet light, so what escapes is the ruddy remainder. You are looking at a star filtered through its own smoke.
card.photoCaption: No photo shows its surface; the color swatch is only a display color. Through binoculars it looks deep orange to red.
card.deeper: Klotz et al. (2013) modeled VLTI/AMBER interferometry with a carbon-star atmosphere: about 3,080–3,170 K, roughly 295 solar radii and 7,000–7,900 solar luminosities, with dust forming close to the star. Gaia EDR3 parallax 4.09 ± 0.21 mas (about 800 light-years); Hipparcos implied about 275 pc. Classed C-N6 (SIMBAD) with B−V near 2.6. GCVS lists small irregular variations (4.8–5.2).

card.question: How can a star almost vanish and return in a single evening?
card.glance: A faint star near the north celestial pole that, every two and a half days, nearly disappears from binoculars for a few hours.
card.whyHere: U Cephei plays Algol’s trick far more deeply, and binoculars let you follow the whole performance from a garden chair.
card.see: U Cephei lies about seven degrees from Polaris toward Cassiopeia’s W; find it with a chart and check the app’s predicted eclipse. Outside eclipse it is an easy binocular star, but near mid-eclipse it sinks to the limit of 50 mm binoculars, and the fade and recovery happen while you watch.
card.understand: U Cep is an eclipsing binary, two stars taking turns hiding each other: a hot blue-white star and a larger, cooler yellow one. The bigger the front star compared with the one behind, and the more squarely it crosses, the deeper the dip, and here the cool star is wide enough to cover its partner almost completely. As in Algol, the cool star has already swollen and spills gas onto its hot partner.
card.wonder: You can watch a star nearly disappear and return in the time it takes to have dinner and a long conversation.
card.connect: RZ Cassiopeiae, not far away, plays the same trick faster but more shallowly.
card.answer: Every 2.49 days the cool star passes almost squarely in front of the hot one, which does most of the shining, so the light drops to about a tenth. Algol only falls to a third; U Cephei comes close to switching off.
card.photoCaption: No photo can show the eclipse; the light-curve sketch shows the typical shape of the dip, not a forecast.
card.deeper: GCVS: Algol-type eclipsing binary, period 2.493091 days, visual range 6.75–9.24. Spectral types B7 Ve + G8 III–IV. Gaia EDR3 parallax 5.194 ± 0.024 mas (about 630 light-years). The hot star shows emission from gas streaming off the cool subgiant; the system is a classic example of mass transfer in a close pair.

superlatives.claim: the first planet found around a Sun-like star

historyHook.text: When its planet was announced in 1995, astronomers were stunned: a giant world circling closer than Mercury, once every four days.

card.question: How do you find a planet that is far too faint to see?
card.glance: A faint yellow star beside the Great Square of Pegasus, a near-twin of the Sun that changed astronomy in 1995.
card.whyHere: 51 Pegasi was the first Sun-like star found to have a planet, and how that planet was found opened the era of worlds around other suns.
card.see: 51 Pegasi lies about one and a half degrees west of the midpoint between Scheat and Markab, the western side of the Great Square. In binoculars it is a modest yellowish point, and you are looking at a sun whose planet you will never see.
card.understand: A planet does not simply circle its star; both circle their shared center of mass, so the star traces a small orbit of its own. As it swings toward us its light shifts slightly blue, and as it swings away slightly red, like the pitch of a passing siren. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi rocking every 4.2 days, the tug of a planet about half Jupiter’s mass, closer to its star than Mercury is to ours.
card.wonder: Its sun is a slightly heavier, brighter and older version of ours, about 4.8 billion years old.
card.connect: A few years later a planet just like it, around HD 209458 in Pegasus, was caught crossing the face of its star.
card.answer: You watch the star instead, and its rhythmic wobble betrays the planet’s pull. Nobody expected a giant world on a four-day orbit, and these “hot Jupiters” forced a rethink of how planetary systems form.
card.photoCaption: No photo can show the planet. Pictures of 51 Pegasi b are artists’ impressions.
card.deeper: Mayor & Queloz (1995) found a 4.23-day radial-velocity signal from Haute-Provence Observatory, implying a planet of at least about half Jupiter’s mass at 0.05 AU (NASA lists 0.052 AU). Metcalfe et al. (2024) combined asteroseismology and spectropolarimetry: 1.09 solar masses, 1.15 solar radii and an age of 4.8 (+0.7/−0.4) billion years. Gaia EDR3 parallax 64.40 mas (50.6 light-years).

exoplanets.method: radial velocity, then the first observed transit

superlatives.claim: the first star seen to dim as its planet passed in front of it

card.question: How can a planet’s shadow tell us how big the planet is?
card.glance: A faint yellow star in western Pegasus, easy in binoculars once a chart has led you to it.
card.whyHere: HD 209458 was the first star seen to dim as its planet crossed in front of it, the method later used by planet-hunting space telescopes.
card.see: Use the app’s chart, because it sits in a sparse patch of western Pegasus roughly between Enif and Matar. It is a steady yellowish point in 50 mm binoculars, and each transit dims it by under two percent, far too little for the eye.
card.understand: The planet’s orbit carries it between us and its star every 3.5 days, an event called a transit. A planet in transit blocks a share of the star’s face equal to its own area divided by the star’s, so the depth of the dip measures its size. In late 1999 two teams caught the dip, about 1.7 percent deep, and since the star’s size was known, the planet’s followed: about 1.36 times Jupiter’s width.
card.wonder: The planet hugs its star so tightly that its atmosphere is boiling away, wrapping it in a long cloud of escaping hydrogen.
card.connect: Thousands of planets have since been found the same way, by spacecraft watching stars for the tiny dip.
card.answer: The dip gave a planet’s width for the first time, and with the wobble supplying its mass, it revealed a giant wider than Jupiter but lighter, a puffed-up world. Starlight filtering through its air during later transits even showed what it is made of.
card.photoCaption: Pictures of this planet are illustrations; no telescope can separate it from its star.
card.deeper: In late 1999 two teams caught the transit: Charbonneau et al. (2000) recorded full transits about 1.7% deep, and Henry et al. (2000) recorded the start of one. Bonomo et al. (2017) give a period of 3.5247 days, 0.68 Jupiter masses and 1.36 Jupiter radii. Ehrenreich et al. (2008) measured an extended hydrogen exosphere around the planet. Gaia EDR3 parallax 20.77 mas (157 light-years).

superlatives.claim: the first Sun-like star found to have more than one planet

card.question: Can another sun hold a whole family of planets, not just one?
card.glance: A modest yellow-white star in Andromeda, a few binocular fields from the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.whyHere: υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star found with more than one planet, the point where single discoveries turned into whole planetary systems.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, move about eight degrees north-east to a modest yellow-white point. Its planets are invisible, but sweep west and the soft glow of the Andromeda Galaxy drifts into view.
card.understand: Like 51 Pegasi, the star wobbles toward and away from us, but its wobble is a tangle, as if several hands were tugging at once. Untangling it is like picking the separate notes out of a chord: one tug repeats in under five days, another about every eight months, a third about every three and a half years. Each rhythm is a planet, and the strength of each tug gives its mass.
card.wonder: The star is a little hotter and larger than the Sun, so its comfortable zone for liquid water lies farther out than Earth’s orbit.
card.connect: One family of worlds 44 light-years away; a few binocular fields west, the Andromeda Galaxy holds hundreds of billions of suns.
card.answer: It can, and υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star shown to: its wobble resolves into three giant planets on very different orbits. From then on, the Sun was no longer the only Sun-like star known to keep a family.
card.photoCaption: No photo can show its planets; the app shows the star’s color and size instead.
card.deeper: Butler et al. (1999) reported the three-planet solution from Lick Observatory and AFOE velocities, with periods of about 4.6, 241 and 1,280 days (the inner planet was announced in 1996–97). Baines et al. (2021) measured 1.57 solar radii and about 6,600 K interferometrically. Gaia EDR3 parallax 74.19 mas (44.0 light-years).

superlatives.claim: the only bright star across a wide, sparse stretch of the southern autumn sky

historyHook.text: In 2008 a dot beside its dust ring was hailed as a planet; it later faded and spread out, most likely debris from a collision.

card.question: What does a planetary system look like while it is still being built?
card.glance: A lone bright white star low in the south on autumn evenings, with nothing as bright for a long way around.
card.whyHere: Fomalhaut is a young, nearby star circled by a wide ring of icy debris, a planetary system still settling down.
card.see: Follow the western side of the Great Square of Pegasus, from Scheat through Markab, and keep going about 45 degrees south. Fomalhaut, in Piscis Austrinus, is the only bright star in that part of the sky, and its ring is far beyond any backyard instrument.
card.understand: Fomalhaut has about twice the Sun’s mass, shines about 16 times brighter and is only about 440 million years old, a tenth of the Sun’s age. Hubble photographed a ring of dust and ice around it roughly 140 times farther out than Earth is from the Sun, with a sharp inner edge. Loose rubble left alone would spread into a fuzzy edge, so a sharp one suggests something is herding it.
card.wonder: Two faint companions, an orange dwarf and a red dwarf, travel with it so far out that one appears several degrees away from it in our sky.
card.connect: The Helix Nebula in Aquarius shows the other end of a star’s life, when it sheds its own ring of material.
card.answer: It looks much like Fomalhaut, a young star wrapped in rings of icy rubble, their edges probably sculpted by the gravity of planets we cannot yet see. The Webb telescope has since found more belts closer in, a system still under construction.
card.photoCaption: Webb’s infrared image shows the dust belts; binoculars show only the bright point at the center.
card.deeper: Mamajek (2012) derived 440 ± 40 million years, 1.92 solar masses and 8,590 K, and Mamajek et al. (2013) showed it forms a very wide triple with the orange dwarf TW PsA and the red dwarf LP 876-10. Hubble imaged the main belt at about 133–158 AU (Kalas et al. 2005). Gáspár & Rieke (2020) reinterpreted “Fomalhaut b” as an expanding dust cloud, and Webb resolved inner belts (Gáspár et al. 2023). Hipparcos parallax 129.8 ± 0.5 mas.

superlatives.claim: the nearest single star of the same type as the Sun (a lone G dwarf)

card.question: How much like the Sun is the nearest lone star of the Sun’s kind?
card.glance: A modest pale-yellow star in Cetus that looks like nothing special, yet is one of the Sun’s nearest look-alikes.
card.whyHere: τ Ceti is the nearest lone star of the Sun’s type, only 12 light-years away, and it shows how varied “Sun-like” can be.
card.see: τ Ceti lies about fifteen degrees east of Diphda, the Whale’s brightest star. In binoculars it is a steady pale-yellow point. Swing back to Diphda, which looks brighter and more orange: that one is a far bigger, farther giant, while τ Ceti is a true dwarf like the Sun.
card.understand: τ Ceti is a yellow dwarf, a star in the steady middle of life like the Sun. Its spectrum shows much weaker lines of iron and other heavy elements than the Sun’s, a sign that it formed from gas less enriched by earlier generations of stars, and earlier usually means older. Its gentle oscillations, read the way seismologists read earthquakes, point to an age of roughly 8 to 10 billion years.
card.wonder: In 1960 it was one of the first two stars ever searched for radio signals from another civilization, in Frank Drake’s Project Ozma.
card.connect: Same color as its neighbor Diphda, a completely different star: color tells you temperature, not size or power.
card.answer: Close, but not a twin: τ Ceti has about 80 percent of the Sun’s mass, under a third of its heavy elements and roughly twice its age. It is less a sibling than an older cousin from a poorer branch of the family.
card.photoCaption: No photo is needed: in every image it is a point. The app’s distance bar shows how close it is.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 273.81 ± 0.17 mas (11.9 light-years). Korolik et al. (2023) give 0.80 solar masses; asteroseismic modeling (Tang & Gai 2011) suggests 8–10 billion years; [Fe/H] ≈ −0.55 (Tuomi et al. 2013). Feng et al. (2017) proposed four small planet candidates with minimum masses of a few Earths; later data have not confirmed all of them, so the app treats them as candidates.

superlatives.claim: one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003

historyHook.text: A Canadian team saw a hint of its planet in 1988, years before planets around other suns were accepted.

card.question: Why did the first hint of a planet around another star take fifteen years to accept?
card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of the house of Cepheus, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.whyHere: Errai is where astronomers first glimpsed a planet’s signal, in 1988, years before anyone was ready to believe in planets around other suns.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the house of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris, and binoculars show it as a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen. Compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the lower corner of the house.
card.understand: Errai is a little heavier than the Sun and has finished burning its core hydrogen, so it is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 a Canadian team noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its speed, the tug a planet would produce. But the surface of a swelling star can pulse, spot and churn, and any of those can fake a wobble.
card.wonder: Its planet, at least one and a half times Jupiter’s mass, circles a star that has a faint red-dwarf partner, so it is a world in a double-star system.
card.connect: In 1995 the planet of 51 Pegasi ended the doubt that Errai’s signal had started.
card.answer: Only years of further measurements could show that the signal kept perfect time like an orbit, and in 2003 a planet on a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed. By then 51 Pegasi had made such planets believable.
card.photoCaption: No photo shows the planet or the close companion; they are hidden in the star’s glare.
card.deeper: Campbell, Walker & Yang (1988) reported a possible long-period signal; Hatzes et al. (2003) confirmed a planet with a period of about 2.5 years and a minimum mass of about 1.7 Jupiters. Knudstrup et al. (2023) use asteroseismology to find about 4,800 K and an age of roughly 5.7 billion years. Gaia EDR3 parallax 72.52 mas (45 light-years). The red-dwarf companion is about 2″ away (WDS).

multiplicity.systemNote: Observed since 1779; the companion has moved a long way around its orbit since then (WDS).

card.question: What would our Sun look like from a neighboring star?
card.glance: A pale yellow star in Cassiopeia’s W with a faint orange companion that steady, high-power binoculars can sometimes split.
card.whyHere: η Cassiopeiae is a near-twin of the Sun only 19 light-years away, which makes it a mirror held up to our own star.
card.see: η Cas sits between Schedar and γ Cas in the W. Its companion is only 13 arcseconds away and far fainter, so most hand-held binoculars show a single star. Brace 10× or larger binoculars on something solid and look for a tiny orange dot pressed against the yellow glare.
card.understand: The bright star is close to a twin of the Sun, slightly hotter, and its companion is a cooler, smaller orange dwarf. Observers have recorded the pair since 1779, and over those centuries the companion has swung a long way around its orbit. Kepler’s laws turn the size and period of an orbit into the mass that drives it, so this slow dance weighs both stars.
card.wonder: Seen from η Cassiopeiae, our Sun would sit in the opposite part of the sky, close to the stars we call the Southern Cross.
card.connect: γ Cas, right beside it in the W and brighter to the eye, is nearly thirty times farther away.
card.answer: Move the Sun out to 19 light-years and it would shine at about the brightness of η Cassiopeiae itself, a modest naked-eye star. Somewhere out there, an observer could be looking at our Sun as just another point in their sky.
card.photoCaption: The survey image shows the bright primary as a saturated disk; the companion is a small point just beside it.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 168.83 mas (19.3 light-years). The WDS records the AB pair from 1779 to 2023, now about 13.5″ apart at magnitudes 3.5 and 7.4. The primary is classed F9 V–G0 V and the companion K7 V. At this distance the Sun (absolute magnitude 4.8) would appear at about magnitude 3.7, close to η Cas A itself.

superlatives.claim: a defining reference star for its class (O9 V)

card.question: What does a newborn heavyweight star look like?
card.glance: A plain-looking blue-white star in little Lacerta, and one of the hottest stars you can see without optics.
card.whyHere: 10 Lacertae is a textbook young, hot, heavy star, so standard that astronomers use it as a reference for the hottest class of stars, the O stars.
card.see: Lacerta’s faint zigzag lies between Cygnus and Andromeda, and 10 Lacertae sits at its southern end. In binoculars it is an unremarkable white point with, at best, a hint of blue. The drama here lies in the numbers rather than the view.
card.understand: 10 Lac has about 22 times the Sun’s mass and a surface near 35,000 K, six times hotter than the Sun’s. You might expect 22 times the mass to give 22 times the light, but the crushing weight on a heavy star’s core drives fusion far harder, so it pours out about 70,000 times the Sun’s light. It spends its fuel thousands of times faster than the Sun, so its whole life is a sprint.
card.wonder: 10 Lacertae began to shine only about three and a half million years ago, when Lucy's kind, the upright-walking apes of East Africa, were already on the move.
card.connect: In a few million years a star this heavy can swell into a red supergiant like the Garnet Star.
card.answer: It looks like 10 Lacertae: a blue-white furnace only a few million years old, whose whole life will be measured in millions of years rather than billions. Stars like this are rare and brief, which is why so few shine in our sky.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point; its heat is measured in its spectrum, not seen in pictures.
card.deeper: Aschenbrenner, Przybilla & Butler (2023) analyzed it with hybrid non-LTE models: 34,550 ± 300 K, 21.6 ± 0.5 solar masses, 7.4 solar radii, about 69,000 solar luminosities and 3.6 million years, at about 550 pc. Sota et al. (2011) use it as the O9 V standard in the Galactic O-Star Spectroscopic Survey. It belongs to the small Lacerta OB1 association.

superlatives.claim: the brightest red dwarf in the night sky

card.question: If most of our neighbors are red dwarfs, why can’t we see any?
card.glance: A dim orange point low in the southern sky, the brightest red dwarf there is and still just below naked-eye view.
card.whyHere: Most of the Sun’s neighbors are red dwarfs, yet none is an easy naked-eye star, and Lacaille 8760, only 13 light-years away, is the brightest of them all.
card.see: Look about twenty degrees west-south-west of Fomalhaut, in Microscopium; from mid-northern sites it stays low, so it rewards a clear southern horizon. In binoculars it is a faint, faintly orange point among other faint stars. Use the chart to be sure which one it is.
card.understand: A red dwarf is a small, cool star, a fraction of the Sun’s mass, and that small mass changes everything. With less weight pressing on its core, fusion runs at a gentle simmer, so it gives off only a small fraction of the Sun’s light and will outlive the Sun many times over. This one is also a flare star, whose magnetic outbursts can briefly brighten it.
card.wonder: It drifts across our sky by about three and a half arcseconds a year, enough to cross a full Moon’s width in roughly five centuries.
card.connect: Fomalhaut, twice as far away, is one of the brightest stars of autumn: nearness alone does not make a star bright.
card.answer: Red dwarfs are simply too feeble: even Lacaille 8760, the brightest of them all, sits just below naked-eye reach. The most common kind of star in the galaxy is the one you never notice.
card.photoCaption: Every photo shows a faint point; its nearness shows up only in how fast it moves against the background.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 251.91 ± 0.04 mas (12.95 light-years) and a proper motion of about 3.45″ per year. SIMBAD classes it M1 V with V = 6.68, which makes it the brightest red dwarf in the sky. GCVS lists it as a UV Ceti-type flare star. It is best seen from latitudes south of about 30° N.

historyHook.text: As Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, Alderamin will take a turn near the north celestial pole around the year 7500.

card.question: What happens to a star that spins once every half day?
card.glance: The brightest star of Cepheus, a white star spinning so fast that it is measurably flattened.
card.whyHere: Alderamin is a star squashed by its own spin, and interferometers have mapped its bulging, cooler waist.
card.see: Alderamin is the bright corner of Cepheus nearest Cygnus, and a line from Schedar through Caph in Cassiopeia leads toward it. In binoculars it is a clean white point. Its flattening is far beyond any optics you own, so the story here lives in the measurements.
card.understand: Alderamin has about twice the Sun’s mass and turns once in roughly 12 hours, where the Sun takes almost a month. At the equator the spin flings material outward, the way spinning pizza dough spreads into a disk, so the star bulges. The CHARA interferometer, combining several telescopes to resolve its tiny disk, has imaged that shape and found the equator dimmer than the poles, because the bulge, farther from the hot core, runs cooler.
card.wonder: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, so the pole star changes over the millennia, and around the year 7500 Alderamin will take its turn as the north star.
card.connect: γ Cassiopeiae, a hotter star, spins hard enough to shed a disk of gas.
card.answer: It flattens, and Alderamin’s equator now stands about 27 percent wider than its pole-to-pole size. A star, it turns out, can have climate zones.
card.photoCaption: No ordinary photo shows its shape; CHARA interferometer reconstructions, a few pixels wide, reveal the flattened disk.
card.deeper: CHARA imaging (Zhao et al. 2009) gives polar and equatorial radii of 2.16 and 2.74 solar radii, a pole-to-equator temperature drop from about 8,560 K to 6,570 K, 1.92 solar masses and an age near 1 billion years. van Belle et al. (2006) measured a projected rotation speed of 283 ± 19 km/s and a period near 12 hours. Hipparcos parallax 66.50 ± 0.11 mas (49 light-years).

card.question: Are two stars that sit side by side in the sky really a pair?
card.glance: Two warm-colored stars side by side at the head of Capricornus, which sharp eyes can split without optics.
card.whyHere: α Capricorni looks like a perfect naked-eye double, and it is a lesson in how flat the sky looks and how deep it really is.
card.see: α Capricorni is the upper star of the Goat’s head in Capricornus, and keen eyes may just split it. Binoculars show two warm-colored stars about a fifth of a Moon’s width apart, with β Capricorni, another wide pair, about two and a half degrees south.
card.understand: To tell a real pair from a chance alignment you need each star’s distance, and Gaia gets it by parallax, watching how much each star shifts as Earth circles the Sun. Hold a finger at arm’s length and blink each eye in turn: the finger jumps more than a distant tree, and near stars jump more than far ones. The brighter star, α², shifts about seven times more than its neighbor.
card.wonder: If both stars sat at the same distance, the fainter one would outshine its neighbor about thirty times over.
card.connect: Sadalsuud, in neighboring Aquarius, is another far-off yellow supergiant.
card.answer: They are not a pair: α² is an orange giant about 110 light-years away, while α¹ is a yellow supergiant roughly 800 light-years away, dim only because it is so far. They merely share a line of sight, an arrangement called an optical double.
card.photoCaption: The survey image shows both stars and their faint field companions; colors in photos are exaggerated compared with the binocular view.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallaxes: α¹ 4.02 ± 0.11 mas (about 810 light-years) and α² 29.91 ± 0.17 mas (about 109 light-years). They are 6.3′ apart (SIMBAD positions). α¹ is classed G3 Ib and α² G9 III. Comparing the apparent magnitudes (4.27 and 3.58) with these distances gives absolute magnitudes of about −2.7 and +1.0, a difference of roughly 30 times in light.

card.question: Which constellation does the Great Square’s brightest corner really belong to?
card.glance: The north-east corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, a bright blue-white star that officially belongs to Andromeda.
card.whyHere: Alpheratz is a hot, bright signpost shared by two constellation figures, and the usual starting point for the hop to the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.see: Alpheratz is the north-east corner of the Great Square, a crisp blue-white point in binoculars. Scheat at the north-west corner gives a fine orange contrast.
card.understand: Alpheratz has an unusually calm atmosphere. With little churning to stir it, gravity and the push of starlight sort the elements the way sediment settles in still water. Heavy ones such as mercury and manganese pile up near the surface, and its spectrum shows those odd amounts plainly.
card.wonder: The Square’s corners are not neighbors: Alpheratz is about half as far away as Scheat.
card.connect: Hot blue-white here and cool orange at Scheat, the Square is a quick lesson in what star colors mean.
card.answer: It belongs to Andromeda, whose head it marks; Pegasus only borrows it to close the Square. The sky’s figures are human patterns laid over stars that never knew they were shared.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 33.62 ± 0.35 mas (97 light-years). Spectral type B8 IV–V HgMn (SIMBAD): a mercury–manganese star in a close binary.

card.question: Can a star that looks perfectly steady actually be pulsing?
card.glance: The western end of Cassiopeia’s W, a bright white star that looks steady to the eye.
card.whyHere: Caph pulses every two and a half hours, far too gently for your eyes, so even a “steady” star can be breathing.
card.see: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-south-west.
card.understand: Caph is a δ Scuti star, one of a family of pulsating stars a little hotter than the Sun. A layer near its surface works like the valve on a pressure cooker, trapping heat, swelling, venting and sinking back. Light meters catch the rhythm as a change of only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.wonder: Caph swells and shrinks slightly, out and back about every two and a half hours, far too gently for the eye to notice.
card.connect: ρ Cassiopeiae, a short hop away, varies far more and lies roughly 170 times farther off.
card.answer: Caph does exactly that, swelling and shrinking about ten times a day, always too little for the eye, so its steadiness is only a limit of our senses.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 59.58 ± 0.38 mas (55 light-years). GCVS: δ Scuti-type, period 0.100 d, range 2.35–2.38.

card.question: Why does Algenib look fainter than the other three corners?
card.glance: A blue-white star a shade fainter than the other corners of the Great Square of Pegasus.
card.whyHere: Algenib is a hot, heavy star that pulses every few hours, and its place in the Square shows how distance can hide power.
card.see: Algenib is the south-east corner of the Great Square. Compare it with Alpheratz at the north-east corner, nearly as bright though not quite.
card.understand: Algenib is a blue-white star many times heavier than the Sun. Its parallax, the tiny shift in its position as Earth orbits the Sun, puts it about 469 light-years away. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star five times farther looks twenty-five times dimmer.
card.wonder: Of the four corners, it is the only one whose light set out before the telescope was invented.
card.connect: Scheat, the cool orange giant at the opposite corner of the Square, is its color opposite.
card.answer: Algenib is roughly five times farther away than Alpheratz yet looks almost as bright, so it must be far more powerful, and the faintest corner is really the mightiest.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 6.95 ± 0.43 mas (about 470 light-years; bright-star parallaxes are less certain). GCVS: β Cephei-type, period 0.152 d, range 2.78–2.89.

card.question: Why does a star only 12 light-years away need binoculars?
card.glance: A faint orange point in northern Andromeda, a red dwarf only about 12 light-years away.
card.whyHere: Groombridge 34 is one of the Sun’s closest neighbors, and a reminder that most nearby stars are dim red dwarfs.
card.see: Use a chart to find it in northern Andromeda; in 50 mm binoculars it is a faint point. Its even fainter partner, 34 arcseconds away, needs a telescope.
card.understand: Two red dwarfs orbit each other here, each a small, cool star a fraction of the Sun’s size. Their nearness shows in their motion, almost three arcseconds a year across our sky. A star that moves that fast against the background is almost always close.
card.wonder: Red dwarfs sip their fuel so slowly that these two will still be shining long after the Sun has died.
card.connect: η Cassiopeiae, a little farther away, is a Sun-like star easy to the naked eye, because the kind of star matters more than nearness.
card.answer: Red dwarfs burn so gently that each gives off only a sliver of the Sun’s light, so even this close the pair stays below naked-eye view, proof that being near is not the same as being bright.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 280.71 mas (11.6 light-years); proper motion about 2.9″ per year. WDS lists the M2 V + M3.5 V pair at 34″ (2019).

card.question: Why is Schedar orange when its neighbors in the W are white?
card.glance: An orange star in Cassiopeia, warmer in tint than its white neighbors in the W.
card.whyHere: Schedar is an aging orange giant, an easy color contrast to the hot blue-white stars in the middle of the W.
card.see: Schedar is the bright southern point of Cassiopeia’s W. Swing to γ Cas at the center of the W and back to compare colors.
card.understand: A star’s color is set by its surface temperature, just as a stove ring glows red before it glows white. Schedar has used up the hydrogen in its core, and as the core contracted, the outer layers swelled. Spread over a much larger surface, the heat escapes from a cooler skin.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 230 years ago, before anyone had measured the distance to any star.
card.connect: Hot blue-white γ Cas, the next bright star east, makes the color contrast plain.
card.answer: Schedar is an aging giant whose swollen surface has cooled to orange. Orange here means cooler than the Sun, not weaker: it still gives off hundreds of times the Sun’s light.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 14.09 ± 0.50 mas (about 230 light-years). Spectral type K0 IIIa (SIMBAD); GCVS lists it as constant after earlier suspicions of variability.

card.question: Can two stars of the same color be completely different?
card.glance: The brightest star of Cetus, a lone orange-yellow star in a sparse part of the southern autumn sky.
card.whyHere: Diphda shares its tint with nearby τ Ceti, proof that color alone cannot tell you what kind of star you are seeing.
card.see: Diphda is the brightest star of Cetus, low in the south on autumn evenings. Compare it with τ Ceti, about fifteen degrees east: a similar tint, very different stars.
card.understand: Color reveals temperature, not size, so the same tint can belong to a small dwarf or a swollen giant. Diphda’s parallax puts it about 96 light-years away, eight times farther than τ Ceti. Yet it still looks brighter, so it must be enormously more powerful.
card.wonder: Diphda is the kind of star that τ Ceti and the Sun will become in billions of years, once their cores run out of hydrogen.
card.connect: τ Ceti, its dim look-alike, is a true dwarf like the Sun.
card.answer: They can, for Diphda is a swollen giant, many times the Sun’s width, while τ Ceti is a small dwarf like the Sun, one color shared by two utterly different lives.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 33.86 ± 0.16 mas (96 light-years). Spectral type G9.5 III (SIMBAD).

card.question: Can binoculars split a pair of stars that truly travel together?
card.glance: A matched pair of white stars in Pisces, 30 arcseconds apart, a test for steady binoculars.
card.whyHere: ψ¹ Piscium is a near-twin pair that steady 10× binoculars can just split, and a real one rather than a chance alignment.
card.see: ψ¹ Piscium lies in Pisces, well south of Mirach; brace your binoculars or use a tripod. At 10× the two white stars touch but separate.
card.understand: How do you tell a real pair from two stars that merely line up? You watch them over time. Observers have measured these two since 1755, and their separation has barely changed, whereas unrelated stars would long since have drifted apart.
card.wonder: Each is a hot white star, both far brighter than the Sun.
card.connect: α Capricorni looks like a pair too, but its stars only line up by chance.
card.answer: Just barely, for the two white stars are 30 arcseconds apart, a fine split for steady 10× binoculars, and centuries of measurement show them moving together as a true pair of suns.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: WDS STF 88 AB: 30.0″ in 2025 (30.4″ in 1755), magnitudes 5.27 and 5.45. Gaia EDR3 parallaxes 10.71 ± 0.60 and 11.38 ± 0.09 mas.

card.question: Why is Mirach the usual starting point for finding two galaxies?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star in Andromeda, the usual stepping stone to the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies.
card.whyHere: Mirach is a cool red giant and a signpost to two neighboring galaxies.
card.see: Mirach is the middle bright star of Andromeda’s chain, a ruddy orange point in binoculars. Hop north-west through μ Andromedae to the Andromeda Galaxy, or the other way to the Triangulum Galaxy.
card.understand: Mirach is a red giant, cooler than the Sun and so redder, but far larger and brighter. Its parallax puts it about 197 light-years away. The galaxies beside it are far too remote for parallax; their distances come from pulsing stars like δ Cephei.
card.wonder: Seen from Mirach, our Sun would be far too faint to find with the naked eye.
card.connect: The Triangulum Galaxy, on the other side of Mirach, is fainter and a little farther still.
card.answer: It happens to sit between them on the sky, so one binocular sweep runs from a star two centuries of light away to galaxies whose light is millions of years old.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 16.52 ± 0.56 mas (about 200 light-years). Spectral type M0 IIIa (SIMBAD).

card.question: Are the five stars of Cassiopeia’s W really neighbors in space?
card.glance: The fourth star of Cassiopeia’s W, a white star about 100 light-years away.
card.whyHere: Ruchbah and its neighbor γ Cas are the simplest way to see that a constellation is a flat picture of deep space.
card.see: Ruchbah is the fourth star of the W, counting from Caph. It looks much like γ Cas next door.
card.understand: A constellation shows only directions, not depths, like a photograph of streetlights in which near and far lamps look alike. Parallax adds the missing dimension, and over a year Ruchbah shifts more than five times as much as γ Cas. A star’s shift shrinks in step with its distance, so Ruchbah is much the closer.
card.wonder: Ruchbah’s light left it about a century ago, while γ Cas’s light set out in the late Middle Ages.
card.connect: γ Cas looks similar only because its far greater power makes up for its distance.
card.answer: Ruchbah lies about 100 light-years away and γ Cas several times deeper, so the W is a letter drawn only for observers on Earth.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 32.81 ± 0.14 mas (99 light-years), versus 5.94 mas for γ Cas. Spectral type A5 IV (SIMBAD).

card.question: Why can’t binoculars split one of the sky’s most famous double stars?
card.glance: A white star at the western tip of Aries, single in binoculars and a perfectly matched pair in a small telescope.
card.whyHere: Mesarthim is a famous matched pair and an honesty check, since some doubles need a telescope rather than binoculars.
card.see: Find the short line of Aries near Hamal; Mesarthim is its faint western end. Binoculars show a single white point, though the twins are only 7 arcseconds apart.
card.understand: How finely you can separate two points depends on the size of the lens and on how much it magnifies. Binoculars magnify only seven to ten times, so stars a few arcseconds apart still look like one point to your eye. A small telescope at higher power opens a dark gap between them.
card.wonder: Seen in a telescope, the pair looks like two headlights side by side.
card.connect: ψ¹ Piscium, nearby, is a real pair that steady binoculars can split.
card.answer: The twins sit far too close together for binoculars and merge into one white point. A small telescope splits them into two near-identical stars.
card.photoCaption: The survey cutout is magnified far beyond any binocular view; the twin pair blends into one point at binocular power.
card.deeper: WDS STF 180: AB 7.3″ (2024), magnitudes 4.52 and 4.58; C at 215″ (8.6). Gaia EDR3 parallax 19.63 mas (166 light-years).

card.question: Why does Sheratan look white beside orange Hamal?
card.glance: The second star of the short line of Aries, a white star near orange Hamal.
card.whyHere: Sheratan and Hamal make an easy two-star lesson in color as temperature.
card.see: Sheratan sits in the short line of Aries, and binoculars show a white point. Swing to Hamal, about four degrees north-east, and compare: white against orange.
card.understand: For a fair color comparison, two stars should be at similar distances behind similar amounts of dust, which reddens starlight. Parallax puts Sheratan about 59 light-years away and Hamal only a little farther. That leaves surface temperature, the physics that makes hot iron glow white and cooler iron orange.
card.wonder: Sheratan is still in its steady adult life, while Hamal has already moved on to its giant years.
card.connect: Hamal, the orange half of this pair, offers a glimpse of the Sun’s possible future.
card.answer: Sheratan’s surface is hotter than Hamal’s, and because the two are near neighbors in depth, the difference is real. You are seeing two temperatures side by side.

card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 55.6 ± 0.6 mas (59 light-years). SIMBAD lists an Am-type spectrum (kA4hA5mA5 V).

card.question: Is the orange pair at the edge of NGC 752 part of that cluster?
card.glance: Two orange stars side by side against a scatter of fainter ones, easy in any binoculars.
card.whyHere: 56 Andromedae looks like part of the star cluster behind it, a good test of how we sort foreground from background.
card.see: Center NGC 752, a large scattering of faint stars in southern Andromeda. The two orange stars at its edge are 56 Andromedae, a clear split in any binoculars.
card.understand: Gaia, the European space mission that measures star distances, watches each star shift as Earth orbits the Sun, and nearer stars shift more. The brighter star shifts several times more than the cluster’s stars, putting it about 330 light-years away, while the fainter shifts only a little more. The cluster lies over a thousand light-years off.
card.wonder: Even the pair is a chance alignment: the fainter star lies more than three times farther away and drifts on its own path.
card.connect: Behind them, NGC 752 is a far older and more distant star family.
card.answer: The two stars only share the cluster’s line of sight, a foreground ornament hung in front of a distant family.
card.photoCaption: The survey cutout shows the pair magnified; in binoculars they sit together at the edge of a faint star cloud.
card.deeper: WDS STFA 4 AB: 202″ (2014), magnitudes 5.8 and 6.1, spectra K0 III and M0 giant. Gaia EDR3 parallaxes 9.96 ± 0.07 mas for A (about 330 light-years) and 2.80 ± 0.08 mas for B, HR 556 (about 1,160 light-years), so the pair is optical.

card.question: How many suns hide in Almach’s single golden point?
card.glance: A bright golden star at the eastern end of Andromeda whose famous blue companion needs a telescope.
card.whyHere: Almach is a gold-and-blue double loved by telescope users, and also the star that matches Algol at full brightness.
card.see: Almach marks the eastern end of Andromeda’s chain of bright stars. Binoculars cannot split its blue companion, under 10 arcseconds away, so use Almach as Algol’s brightness yardstick instead.
card.understand: The golden star is a giant, swollen and cooled late in life. Its blue companion looked single until finer measurements broke it into a close pair, and one of those proved double too, revealed by the rhythmic shift of its spectral lines. Each layer needed a sharper tool than the last.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 400 years ago, around the time Galileo first turned a telescope on the sky.
card.connect: If Algol looks fainter than Almach tonight, Algol is in eclipse.
card.answer: There are at least four, the golden giant and a blue companion that is itself three hot stars, a small family of suns in one point of light.
card.photoCaption: The survey cutout shows a single bright disk; the blue companion is lost in the glare at this scale.
card.deeper: WDS STF 205: A–BC 9.5″ (2024), magnitudes 2.3 and 5.0; BC is a 0.4″ pair, and B is itself a spectroscopic binary. Hipparcos parallax 8.30 ± 1.04 mas (roughly 350–450 light-years).

card.question: What might the Sun look like a few billion years from now?
card.glance: A warm orange point, the brightest star in the small constellation of Aries.
card.whyHere: Hamal is a nearby orange giant, a glimpse of the Sun’s possible future in a few billion years.
card.see: Hamal leads the short line of Aries, east of the Great Square. Compare it with white Sheratan, four degrees south-west.
card.understand: A star like the Sun spends most of its life fusing hydrogen in its core. When that runs out, the core contracts and heats up, a shell around it starts burning, and the extra heat pushes the outer layers outward. The star swells, and its larger surface cools toward orange.
card.wonder: It is close for a giant: its light left it about 66 years ago.
card.connect: White Sheratan, at nearly the same distance, makes the color comparison fair.
card.answer: Something like Hamal, an orange giant many times the Sun’s width, grown large and cool after its core ran dry. You are looking at one of the Sun’s possible tomorrows.

card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 49.56 ± 0.25 mas (66 light-years). Spectral type K2 IIIb (SIMBAD).

card.question: Are the two faint stars beside 14 Arietis its true companions?
card.glance: A modest white star in Aries with two faint companions about a minute and a half of arc away.
card.whyHere: 14 Arietis is a test of steady binoculars, and a reminder that not every pair of stars on the sky is a pair in space.
card.see: 14 Arietis lies east of Hamal; brace 10×50 binoculars under a dark sky. Look for two faint points flanking the white star at about 100 arcseconds.
card.understand: Catalogs of double stars list any close pairing an observer noted, real or not. To prove a partnership you need shared motion over decades or matching distances. Many “doubles” in such catalogs turn out to be stars that simply happen to line up.
card.wonder: William Herschel listed this trio long ago, and the question he could not answer is still open.
card.connect: ψ¹ Piscium, nearby, is a pair whose stars are known to travel together.
card.answer: Nobody knows yet, because although the two faint stars sit about 100 arcseconds from the white one, no one has shown that they share its motion or its distance.
card.photoCaption: The survey cutout is magnified; in binoculars the companions are faint points at the edge of visibility.
card.deeper: WDS H 6 69: AB 93″ and AC 106″ (magnitudes about 8.0). Gaia DR2 parallax 18.97 ± 0.68 mas (about 170 light-years).

card.question: How much farther is the Triangulum Galaxy than the star beside it?
card.glance: The brightest star of little Triangulum, a white star about 130 light-years away.
card.whyHere: β Trianguli is a signpost star near the faint Triangulum Galaxy, and together they span an enormous jump in depth.
card.see: Triangulum’s three stars form a slim triangle just south of Andromeda, and β Trianguli is the brightest of them. Binoculars show a white point, with the Triangulum Galaxy a short hop west.
card.understand: β Tri is a white star a little past its steady adult phase. Its parallax puts it about 127 light-years away. The galaxy nearby is far too remote for parallax; its distance comes from the same pulsing stars that first measured the Andromeda Galaxy’s.
card.wonder: β Trianguli is really two stars, too close for any telescope to split, revealed only because the lines in its spectrum shift back and forth.
card.connect: The Triangulum Galaxy’s faint glow lies a short hop west.
card.answer: More than ten thousand times farther: the star’s light is about 130 years old, while the faint glow beside it left millions of years ago, before our species existed.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 25.71 ± 0.34 mas (127 light-years). Spectral type A5 III (SIMBAD).
