card.question: What do binoculars show of one of the north’s finest triple stars?
card.glance: A white star east of Cassiopeia’s W, single in binoculars and a fine triple in a telescope.
card.whyHere: ι Cassiopeiae is an honest reminder that this beautiful triple belongs to the telescope; in binoculars you see only the combined light.
card.see: ι Cassiopeiae lies about five degrees north-east of ε Cassiopeiae, the eastern end of the W. Binoculars show one white point, while the triple needs a telescope.
card.understand: Three stars orbit together here, separated by only a few arcseconds. Binoculars magnify seven to ten times, which still leaves a gap of a few arcseconds far finer than your eye can resolve, so all three merge into one. The brightest is a peculiar white star with unusually strong strontium in its spectrum.
card.wonder: Telescope users rate it one of the finest triple stars in the northern sky.
card.connect: η Cassiopeiae, back in the W, is a double that braced binoculars can sometimes split.
card.answer: Binoculars find it but cannot open it: to them ι Cassiopeiae is one white point, and only a telescope reveals the family inside.
card.photoCaption: The magnified survey cutout merges the triple into one bright disk.
card.deeper: WDS STF 262: AB 3.0″ and AC 6.9″ (2022), magnitudes 4.7, 6.9 and 9.1. Hipparcos parallax 24.55 ± 0.81 mas (about 130 light-years).

card.question: What does a typical star in the Sun’s neighborhood look like?
card.glance: A faint orange dwarf in Cetus, just visible to the eye under a dark sky and easy in binoculars with a chart.
card.whyHere: HD 16160 is a nearby orange dwarf, smaller and cooler than the Sun, the kind of modest star that fills our neighborhood.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about seven degrees west-north-west of Menkar, the Whale’s orange nose star. In binoculars it is a modest yellow-orange point.
card.understand: An orange dwarf is smaller and cooler than the Sun and burns its fuel so slowly that it will outlive the Sun by billions of years. This one creeps across our sky by over two arcseconds a year, a telltale sign of a close neighbor. Parallax confirms it.
card.wonder: Its light left about 24 years ago, so you see it as it was a generation back.
card.connect: τ Ceti, half as far away, is a closer neighbor more like the Sun.
card.answer: Smaller, cooler and dimmer than the Sun: HD 16160 is just visible to the eye, and the red dwarfs that outnumber it are fainter still.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 138.34 mas (23.6 light-years). Spectral type K3 V (SIMBAD).

card.question: Can you watch a complete eclipse of a star in one evening?
card.glance: A faint white star in northern Cassiopeia that fades to about a quarter of its light every 28.7 hours.
card.whyHere: RZ Cassiopeiae is a quick eclipsing pair, dipping more than twice as often as Algol.
card.see: Find it with a chart near the Cassiopeia–Camelopardalis border, north of the W, and check the predicted eclipse time. Compare it with nearby stars of similar brightness before and during the dip.
card.understand: Two stars orbit each other every 1.2 days and take turns passing in front of each other, a miniature Algol. The closer two stars are, the faster they orbit, and these two are so close that a circuit takes barely more than a day. That keeps each eclipse brief too.
card.wonder: Its light takes about 213 years to reach us, so the eclipse you watch tonight happened long before you were born.
card.connect: Algol, the bright original, plays the same trick at naked-eye brightness.
card.answer: You can, as one star slips in front of the other and the light sinks to about a quarter and climbs back, all within a few hours.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: GCVS: Algol-type, period 1.19525 d, range 6.18–7.72. Gaia EDR3 parallax 15.31 mas (213 light-years).

card.question: What does a red giant look like when it is not pulsing?
card.glance: The orange-red star in the head of Cetus, the Whale.
card.whyHere: Menkar is a red giant that keeps its light steady, which makes it the perfect partner for restless Mira.
card.see: Menkar marks the head of Cetus, a ruddy point with a wide, faint blue-white star close by. Compare its color with Mira when Mira is visible.
card.understand: Menkar is a red giant, an old star swollen large with a cool surface, much like Mira. The difference is the stage. Mira has reached a later, unstable phase in which its outer layers rock in and out, while Menkar’s are still settled.
card.wonder: Its light left about 250 years ago, around the time of the American Revolution.
card.connect: Mira, in the Whale’s neck, shows what a giant like Menkar may become when its outer layers start to swing.
card.answer: It looks like Menkar, the same cool, ruddy kind of star as Mira, but holding its light steady while Mira swings more than a thousandfold.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 13.09 ± 0.44 mas (about 250 light-years). Spectral type M1.5 IIIa (SIMBAD).

card.question: Can a pair of stars eclipse each other only once in many years?
card.glance: A yellow star in the arc of Perseus, between Mirfak and Cassiopeia.
card.whyHere: γ Persei is a yellow giant with a hidden hot companion, a pair that lines up so rarely that each eclipse is an event.
card.see: γ Persei sits in the curving arc of Perseus, between Mirfak and Cassiopeia’s W, in a rich Milky Way field. Sweep on to Mirfak and its cluster.
card.understand: Its light combines a yellow giant and a hotter white companion on a wide orbit. The wider an orbit, the longer each lap takes, and the less likely we are to see it edge-on. Here we do, and catalogs list the pair as eclipsing.
card.wonder: Each rare eclipse is precious, because it lets astronomers measure both stars as one slides behind the other.
card.connect: Algol, a few degrees south, is the opposite case: an eclipse every few days.
card.answer: They can, and γ Persei’s two stars line up for us so seldom that most observers never see an eclipse, Algol’s geometry stretched across years.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 14.13 ± 0.77 mas (about 230 light-years). SIMBAD: G9 III + A2; GCVS type EA/GS.

card.question: What does a heavy star look like as it starts to swell?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Perseus with a faint companion lost in its glare.
card.whyHere: ζ Persei is a young blue supergiant, a heavy star at the very start of its swollen stage.
card.see: ζ Persei marks the southern foot of Perseus, north of the Pleiades. Its 9th-magnitude companion, 13 arcseconds away, hides in the glare.
card.understand: ζ Per is a blue supergiant, a hot, heavy star whose core hydrogen is running low. The core contracts and the envelope begins to expand while the surface still glows blue-white. Heavy stars hurry through this stage, so catching one here is like seeing a sprinter mid-stride.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 800 years ago, in the Middle Ages.
card.connect: Mirfak, higher in Perseus, is a heavy star a little further along, already cooled to yellow-white.
card.answer: It looks like ζ Persei, still hot and blue-white but already expanding, a star that will live only tens of millions of years.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 3.86 ± 0.42 mas (roughly 760–950 light-years; bright-star parallaxes are less certain). WDS AB 12.8″, magnitudes 2.9 and 9.2.

card.question: How faint does Algol get at the bottom of an eclipse?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Perseus, a handy yardstick for Algol.
card.whyHere: ε Persei is the star Algol matches at the bottom of an eclipse, your gauge for how deep it has gone.
card.see: ε Persei lies a few degrees east of Algol, and binoculars show a blue-white point. Compare Algol with it while an eclipse is under way.
card.understand: Observers judge brightness by comparison, because the eye is poor at absolute brightness but good at telling which of two stars is fainter. ε Per itself throbs by only about a tenth of a magnitude. That makes it a fair ruler to hold against Algol.
card.wonder: It is about seven times farther away than Algol.
card.connect: Algol at full light matches Almach instead, so between the two yardsticks you can follow the whole eclipse.
card.answer: About as faint as ε Persei: when the two match, the eclipse is at its deepest. Watching the gap between them close and reopen is the whole eclipse in miniature.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 5.33 ± 0.43 mas (about 570–670 light-years). GCVS: β Cephei-type, range 2.88–3.00.

superlatives.claim: the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars

card.question: Can a star pulse every few hours without anyone noticing?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.whyHere: β Cephei names a whole class of hot pulsating stars and is the opposite of δ Cephei, its cool, slow, deep-pulsing neighbor.
card.see: β Cephei lies in Cepheus between Alderamin and Errai, and binoculars show a blue-white point. Its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, needs a small telescope.
card.understand: Deep in β Cep’s layers, iron atoms trap heat when squeezed and release it when they expand, and that valve keeps the star ringing like a bell. The ringing shows up as a rhythm in its light and in the speed of its surface. Its light changes by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.wonder: Alfirk rings like a bell several times a day, and astronomers read that ringing the way seismologists read earthquakes, to probe the hidden inside of a hot star.
card.connect: δ Cephei, in the same constellation, pulses slowly and deeply enough to follow by eye.
card.answer: It can, and for most of history nobody noticed, since β Cephei rings every 4.57 hours too faintly for any eye.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 4.76 ± 0.30 mas (about 690 light-years). GCVS: β Cephei-type, period 0.19048 d, range 3.12–3.17. WDS STF 2806 AB 13.5″, magnitudes 3.2 and 8.6.

card.question: What is the brightest star of Aquarius really like?
card.glance: The brightest star of Aquarius, a pale yellow star in a faint region.
card.whyHere: Sadalsuud is a yellow supergiant, close in type to its neighbor Sadalmelik, two powerful stars side by side.
card.see: Sadalsuud is the brightest star of Aquarius, in a quiet stretch of sky east of Capricornus, and binoculars show a pale yellow point. Sadalmelik, a similar star, lies about ten degrees north-east.
card.understand: Sadalsuud is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life, with the Sun’s color but vastly greater size. We know it is no nearby Sun-like star from its distance: parallax puts it about 546 light-years away. A star that looks this bright from that far must far outshine the Sun.
card.wonder: Seen from Sadalsuud, our Sun would be too faint to find even with binoculars.
card.connect: Sadalmelik, its look-alike, sits ten degrees away at a similar distance.
card.answer: It is a yellow supergiant: the Sun’s color, but a heavy star swollen vastly larger and brighter. Its light has been traveling for more than five centuries to reach you.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 5.97 ± 0.21 mas (about 550 light-years). Spectral type G0 Ib (SIMBAD).

card.question: How red can a star look through binoculars?
card.glance: A deep red carbon star near the pole, visible in binoculars only around its peak.
card.whyHere: S Cephei is one of the reddest stars in the northern sky, a carbon-rich giant that pulses like Mira.
card.see: Check its current brightness first, because it spends much of its cycle out of binocular reach. Near peak it is a striking blood-red point in northern Cepheus.
card.understand: Like TX Piscium, S Cep has carbon dredged up from deep inside onto its surface, where it forms molecules that soak up blue light. Like Mira, it pulses, swelling and shrinking over many months. Its 484-day cycle carries it from near naked-eye visibility to far below binocular reach.
card.wonder: Its cycle lasts about 16 months, so its peaks drift through the calendar from year to year.
card.connect: TX Piscium, a carbon star you can see any night, shows the same color more gently.
card.answer: Blood red, at its peak: carbon strips the blue from its light, and its pulse brings it within reach for only part of each cycle.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: GCVS: Mira-type, period 484 d, range 6.6–12.5, spectral type C7,4e. Gaia EDR3 parallax 2.05 ± 0.07 mas (about 1,600 light-years).

card.question: Where does the bright orange nose of Pegasus point?
card.glance: A clear orange star in Pegasus, out on its own west of the Great Square.
card.whyHere: Enif is an orange supergiant and the jumping-off point for the globular cluster M15.
card.see: Enif marks the nose of the flying horse. M15 lies about four degrees north-west, a fuzzy round star in the same direction.
card.understand: Enif is a supergiant, a heavyweight that has ballooned in old age into a cool orange giant. Heavy stars burn through their fuel fast, so Enif is young in years though already near its end. At about 690 light-years, it must be vastly brighter than the Sun to look this bright.
card.wonder: The light you see from Enif left it in the 1300s, before printing came to Europe.
card.connect: The Great Square of Pegasus lies a short sweep to the north-east, its four corners a lesson in how distance hides power.
card.answer: It points to M15, an ancient ball of stars, so one binocular sweep runs from young, heavy Enif to some of the oldest stars in the Galaxy.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 4.73 ± 0.17 mas (about 690 light-years). Spectral type K2 Ib–II (SIMBAD).

card.question: Can every eclipsing star be seen to change by eye?
card.glance: The brightest star of Capricornus, at the Goat’s tail.
card.whyHere: Deneb Algedi is a nearby eclipsing pair whose dips are real but too shallow to judge easily by eye.
card.see: Deneb Algedi marks the tail of Capricornus, a white point in binoculars. Its eclipses are shallow, so try only when the app predicts one.
card.understand: Two stars orbit each other here about once a day, and when one passes in front of the other the light drops. How deep the dip goes depends on how much of the brighter star gets covered, and here only a small part is hidden. Catching it takes good comparison stars and patience.
card.wonder: Only about 39 light-years away, it is one of the nearest eclipsing pairs visible to the naked eye.
card.connect: Algol, the classic eclipsing star, shows what a deep dip looks like.
card.answer: Not every one, and Deneb Algedi dips only by about a quarter of a magnitude, while Algol’s eclipses, five times deeper, are the easy kind.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: GCVS: Algol-type, period 1.0228 d, range 2.81–3.05. Hipparcos parallax 84.27 ± 0.19 mas (39 light-years).

card.question: Can a star share the Sun’s color and yet be vastly bigger?
card.glance: A pale yellow star near the Water Jar asterism of Aquarius.
card.whyHere: Sadalmelik is a yellow supergiant, the same color as the Sun but enormously more powerful.
card.see: Sadalmelik lies in Aquarius about ten degrees north-east of Sadalsuud, and binoculars show a pale yellow point. The small Y-shaped Water Jar lies just to the east.
card.understand: A star’s color reports its surface temperature, so a yellow star is roughly as hot as the Sun on the surface. Parallax puts Sadalmelik about 660 light-years away, and to look this bright from that far it must pour out vastly more light than the Sun. The same temperature and far more light can only mean a far bigger surface.
card.wonder: It sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, the sky’s projection of Earth’s equator.
card.connect: Sadalsuud, ten degrees south-west, is its near twin.
card.answer: It can, for Sadalmelik is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star ballooned in old age to enormous size and power, and color reads temperature, never size.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 4.95 ± 0.43 mas (about 610–720 light-years). Spectral type G2 Ib (SIMBAD).

card.question: What hides inside Matar’s yellow glow?
card.glance: A yellow star in the “leg” of Pegasus, north-west of Scheat.
card.whyHere: Matar is a yellow bright giant with a hidden companion, a waypoint across northern Pegasus.
card.see: Matar lies about five degrees north-west of Scheat, in the foreleg of Pegasus, and binoculars show a yellowish point. Compare its tint with orange Scheat.
card.understand: Matar is an aging giant star, and its spectrum, the star’s light spread into colors, holds a surprise. Mixed in with the giant’s lines are the signatures of a hotter, smaller star. The two are too close to separate with any binoculars, so the light itself is the only witness.
card.wonder: Its light left about two centuries ago, around when Charles Darwin set sail on the Beagle.
card.connect: Scheat, at about the same distance, is a cooler, redder giant.
card.answer: A hotter companion, too close to see, betrayed only by its fingerprints in the combined light of the aging yellow giant. Many single-looking stars turn out to be pairs this way.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 16.63 ± 0.70 mas (about 200 light-years). SIMBAD: G8 II + F0 V.

card.question: What does color tell you in a two-star binocular field?
card.glance: An orange star and a white one, about two-thirds of a degree apart in Aquarius, a color pair for binoculars.
card.whyHere: τ Aquarii is a ready-made lesson in what star colors mean, all in one binocular field.
card.see: Find the orange star τ² Aquarii, south of the Water Jar; the white τ¹ lies about two-thirds of a degree to its south-west. Defocus slightly and the colors bloom.
card.understand: A star’s color tells its surface temperature: cooler surfaces glow red and orange, hotter ones white and blue. Defocusing spreads each star’s light into a small disk, giving the color-sensing cells of your eye more to work with. Distance is no explanation here, since Gaia puts the two at similar distances, about 330 and 360 light-years.
card.wonder: The orange giant is much the brighter of the two despite its cooler surface, because it is so much larger.
card.connect: α Capricorni, nearby, is a pair that is pure line-of-sight chance.
card.answer: It tells you temperature, for τ² is a cool orange giant and τ¹ a hot white star still in its prime, though whether the two are related is unknown.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: SIMBAD: τ¹ Aqr B9 V (V 5.68), τ² Aqr M0 III (V 3.98), separated by 39′. Gaia EDR3 parallaxes 9.13 ± 0.06 and 10.02 ± 0.17 mas.

card.question: Why does Scheat glow orange when the Square’s other corners are white?
card.glance: An orange-red star that stands out from the white corners of the Great Square of Pegasus.
card.whyHere: Scheat is a cool red giant among hot blue-white corners, the one splash of color in the Great Square.
card.see: Scheat is the north-west corner of the Great Square. Swing to Markab, the corner directly south, and back: orange against blue-white.
card.understand: Scheat is a red giant late in life, swollen so large that its surface has cooled far below the Sun’s temperature. Giants this cool and this large are rarely perfectly steady, and Scheat wanders irregularly by a few tenths of a magnitude. Its light is crossed by broad bands of molecules that can only survive in a cool atmosphere.
card.wonder: It sits twice as far as Alpheratz and less than half as far as Algenib, so the Square is a shape only from here.
card.connect: Markab, the Square’s south-west corner, shows the hot end of the same scale.
card.answer: Scheat’s swollen surface is cool enough to glow orange-red, while the Square’s other corners are hot blue-white stars, so one glance around the Square spans two very different temperatures.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 16.64 ± 0.15 mas (196 light-years). GCVS: irregular, 2.31–2.74. Spectral type M2.5 II–III (SIMBAD).

card.question: Why does Markab look white beside orange Scheat?
card.glance: A crisp blue-white star at one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.
card.whyHere: Markab is a hot blue-white star, the color opposite of orange Scheat.
card.see: Markab is the Square’s south-west corner. Compare it with Scheat directly north: white against orange.
card.understand: Markab is a hot white star just beginning to leave its long, steady adult phase. Its surface is far hotter than Scheat’s, so its light peaks toward the blue end of the spectrum. Parallax puts it about 133 light-years away, closer than Scheat, so distance plays no part in the difference.
card.wonder: Like Algenib and Alpheratz, it is a hot star, which makes orange Scheat the odd one out of the Square.
card.connect: Scheat, at the Square’s next corner north, completes the color contrast.
card.answer: Markab’s surface is much hotter: it is a white star still near the prime of life, while Scheat is a cool red giant near its end. The two corners are two different chapters of stellar life.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 24.46 ± 0.19 mas (133 light-years). Spectral type A0 IV (SIMBAD).

superlatives.claim: one of the fastest-moving stars across our sky

card.question: Why is one of the Sun’s nearest neighbors invisible to the eye?
card.glance: A faint orange point in Piscis Austrinus, south of Fomalhaut, a red dwarf about 11 light-years away.
card.whyHere: Lacaille 9352 is one of the nearest stars to the Sun and one of the fastest-moving across our sky.
card.see: From Fomalhaut, go about six degrees south and use a chart. In binoculars it is a faint point, and from northern sites it stays low.
card.understand: A red dwarf is a star smaller, cooler and far dimmer than the Sun. This one gives away its nearness by racing across our sky faster than almost any other star, and stars that move that fast are almost always close. Parallax confirms it.
card.wonder: It moves about seven arcseconds a year, a full Moon’s width in under three centuries.
card.connect: Fomalhaut, more than twice as far away, is hundreds of times brighter.
card.answer: Lacaille 9352 is a red dwarf, so even at about 11 light-years it is too faint to see without binoculars. Our nearest neighbors are mostly quiet little stars like this.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 304.14 mas (10.7 light-years); proper motion about 6.9″ per year. Spectral type M2 V (SIMBAD; often given as M0.5 V).

card.question: Can binoculars show a double star whose stars are 3 arcseconds apart?
card.glance: A yellow-orange giant in northern Cepheus whose close companion needs a telescope.
card.whyHere: ο Cephei is a yellow giant with a close partner, an honest example of a double that binoculars show as one star.
card.see: Find ο Cephei with a chart in northern Cepheus, and binoculars show a single warm-colored point. The companion is only 3 arcseconds away.
card.understand: The giant and its fainter companion circle each other slowly, and telescopes have tracked the pair for generations. Binoculars magnify seven to ten times, which stretches a gap this small to far less than the eye can separate. A small telescope at higher power is the minimum tool for this one.
card.wonder: Its light left about 200 years ago, around when the first steam railways opened.
card.connect: ψ¹ Piscium is a pair that steady binoculars really can split.
card.answer: This one does not: its companion sits too close to the giant, so binoculars show only their combined light. Knowing which doubles lie beyond your optics saves a lot of squinting.
card.photoCaption: The magnified survey cutout merges the pair into one bright disk.
card.deeper: WDS STF 3001 AB: 3.0″ (2025), magnitudes 5.0 and 7.3. Hipparcos parallax 16.06 ± 0.36 mas (about 200 light-years).

card.question: How can a star 9,000 light-years away still reach the naked eye?
card.glance: A faint white star near the cluster M52 in Cassiopeia.
card.whyHere: 6 Cassiopeiae is a white supergiant about 9,000 light-years away that still reaches naked-eye brightness under dark skies.
card.see: Find the cluster M52 west of Caph. 6 Cas is a modest white star about three degrees east of it, in the same rich Milky Way field.
card.understand: 6 Cas is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life. Its distance comes from the stars it travels with, a loose group whose members can be measured together. To look as bright as it does from that far, it must shine tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun.
card.wonder: A close companion, too near to split in binoculars, travels with it.
card.connect: ρ Cassiopeiae, at a similar distance, is just as extreme.
card.answer: Only a supergiant’s power could cross that gulf and still reach your eye, and the light you see set out about 9,000 years ago.
card.photoCaption: No photo is shown: in any image this star is just a point. The app shows its color and place on the star diagram instead.
card.deeper: Kasikov et al. (2026) adopt a group-based distance of 2.79 ± 0.07 kpc. SIMBAD lists A2.5 Ia + O9.8 II; WDS shows a 1.5″ companion.

card.question: How far away is the hot star that marks the way to Caroline’s Rose?
card.glance: A blue-white star beside the misty cluster Caroline’s Rose, with a close companion that needs a telescope.
card.whyHere: σ Cassiopeiae is a hot young star next to an old cluster, a handy marker for the old cluster Caroline’s Rose.
card.see: σ Cassiopeiae lies south-west of Caph, just south of ρ Cassiopeiae, and binoculars show a blue-white point. The soft glow of Caroline’s Rose sits about a degree to the north.
card.understand: σ Cas is a hot blue-white star, many times heavier than the Sun, with a close companion 3 arcseconds away. Its parallax is smaller than its own uncertainty, so the star is far away but nobody can say how far. Comparing its spectrum with stars of known power gives a rough answer.
card.wonder: Young and blue beside an old cluster, it is a chance meeting of two very different ages on one line of sight.
card.connect: The misty cluster beside it is a star family that lost its hottest members long ago.
card.answer: Nobody knows precisely: thousands of light-years, with a large uncertainty, and sometimes the most honest number in astronomy comes with wide error bars.
card.photoCaption: The magnified survey cutout merges the pair into one disk.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 0.72 ± 0.43 mas is too uncertain for a reliable distance. WDS STF 3049 AB: 2.9″, magnitudes 5.0 and 7.2.
